articles.text: The entire plant of the Miles City Dressed Beef Co. was destroyed by fire Tuesday. The loss was $15,000. No insurance. We are unable to learn anything of the plans of the company but as there was considerable difficulty about their cattle contracts it seems probable that they will not rebuild.
articles.summary: Fire destroyed the Miles City Dressed Beef Co. plant, a $15,000 uninsured loss.

articles.text: The long continued hot weather has about dried up the green feed that was to be used at the experimental fattery here but feeding will begin very soon on twenty or thirty head. In the series of experiments in New York, one yearling increased in one hundred days from 840 to 1120 pounds and was then sold at a top price for beef.
articles.summary: Hot weather has dried up green feed for the experimental fattery at Medora, but feeding of twenty or thirty head will begin soon.

articles.text: Last Saturday, a hail storm east of Dickinson did severe damage to the crops. Beginning a few miles east of Dickinson and extending beyond Glen Ullin, it is estimated that over a thousand acres of standing grain was completely ruined. The most of it was insured. The evening passenger train met the storm near Hebron and over seventy-five panes of heavy window glass were broken out.
articles.summary: A hail storm from east of Dickinson to beyond Glen Ullin ruined over a thousand acres of grain and broke train windows near Hebron.

articles.text: We have before had occasion to allude to the weak arguments employed by the Western Rural in its articles against the range cattle industry. It was one of the leaders of the eastern agricultural press a few months ago in an endeavor to compel range cattlemen to lease the land they occupied. As any reasonable man should have foreseen, the selfish animus of the crusade was so manifest that it fell of its own weight. There were no arguments in right or justice to support it. Now, however, the Western Rural speaks of cowmen as "interlopers." An interloper is one who meddles in business in which he has no concern. The only possible way in which this term can apply to rangemen is that their product, by coming into competition with stall-fed cattle, makes them "interlopers." Grant that in this sense they are interlopers and what does it prove? By the Rural's own words they are interlopers because they compete in open market for business. An argument then, based on such a foundation, would totally destroy all business principles. Competition is not only the life of trade, but in this case, competition is the greatest boon imaginable to the poorer classes of the United States. There is no need of an array of figures to prove that the range cattle industry has decreased the price of meat so that it is now a regular food for poor men, where an advance of a few cents a pound would put it in the list of luxuries, seldom or never to be tasted. Suppose that the Rural's expressed wish should be realized and that "our farms produce all the cattle for which there is such a demand." The utter folly of such a statement and wish is so apparent as scarcely to need explanation. If eastern farmers could supply the beef demand, why in the world don't they do it? The Rural's answer would be "they can't do it at the cheap price of the range beef." They couldn't possibly do it anyway, but take the Rural's answer as final and we have an astonishing boomerang of a social science argument that an industry should be annihilated for the benefit of a small number of men, which, by its existence, saves millions of dollars a year to consumers. But to prop up its argument, the Rural would say, this business is made possible because it is conducted on land that belongs to the United States. Would it be better to stop this food supply, to the detriment of every man, woman and child in the country, because rent is not paid for for the use of land that no one else wants? The Rural's arguments are too narrow and selfish to find many adherents. It argues for a small class against all the rest of the people, a position perfectly untenable under a republican form of government. In conclusion we would tell the Rural that the very fact of its existence is one of the strongest points in its favor. No such abuse as the Rural claims the range industry to be, could keep its footing in the United States. It would long since have been annihilated by legislative enactment.
articles.summary: Packard rebuts the Western Rural's attacks on the range cattle industry and its description of cowmen as "interlopers."

articles.headline: Conclusions About Cattle Feeding.
articles.text:
After some protracted experiments in cattle feeding at the Illinois State university, Prof. G. E. Morrow says: Bearing in mind that it is not wise to draw final conclusions from single trials, the fact concerning these cattle suggest or illustrate, among other things, that:

1. The difference in animals of like breeding, and under like treatment is often greater than those in typical animals of different breeds.

2. Under the prevalent methods of wintering steers in the western states, little or no gain is made in weight during winter.

3. It is difficulty, if not impossible, to secure under good conditions, gains in winter which shall nearly equal those made in summer.

4. The largest gains may be expected from animals in thin flesh, if in good health. It is difficult to secure rapid gain in weight during continued feeding.

5. Under like conditions young animals make largest gain in proportion of food eaten.

6. A fair profit can be made at present low prices by grazing, and then grain feeding for two or three months, cattle which have been judiciously bought or economically reared, to be sold when from 30 to 36 months old.

7. Economy of production is quite as important as maximum product, especially in times of low prices. It is not clear that it is profitable to give full grain feeding to steers, designed for the general market, during the best of the grazing season. It is not proven that it is most profitable for western farmers to fatten and sell steers as yearlings.
articles.summary: Prof. G. E. Morrow's conclusions from cattle-feeding experiments at the Illinois State university (reprinted).

articles.headline: Glanders.
articles.text:
As considerable alarm exists throughout the country at the present time concerning the spread of glanders, a brief history of its cause, and the best method of prevention may be valuable to horse-owners.

The principal cause of this incurable disease, says Dr. Pelton, is tight, foul stables. It is contagious by inoculation. Farcy is a different form or stage of the same disease, and the horse never dies of either until both forms are fully developed. But if farcy appears first it may be cured by correct and prompt treatment.

Mr. Hinds, an English veterinary writer, cites an instance where three hundred cavalry horses were put below decks during a storm at sea, and the hatchways closed, and when taken out thirty-six hours afterwards, all were found to have taken either glanders or farcy, and they were all thrown overboard.

Glanders first shows itself by staring coat, and slight discharge (thin and glutinous from the left nostril, and never from the right nostril. Small white blisters soon appear a little upon the membranes of the left nostril, and the glands of the under jaw on that side become somewhat enlarged and hard. Let no man handle such a case unless his hands are sound and free from any scratch or sore, for the matter coming in contact with a raw place, or membrane, will communicate the disease to man as readily as to a horse. But if the hands are sound, put your finger up the left nostril to make sure it is a white blister on the membrane, and if it proves to be so, destroy the unfortunate animal at once. But it must be remembered, that nasal gleet is often mistaken for glanders. It is readily cured by a skillful veterinarian, and is not contagious. It is caused generally by out-door exposure, and the discharge, in bad cases, is very profuse from both nostrils, usually a light straw color, often streaked with blood, when running to grass.

Farcy causes a staring coat, and some other symptoms of glanders, but its certain symptoms are what are called farcy buds—small, round, hard swellings on the inside of the legs and thighs, belly, and often about the throat and under jaw; sometimes only in one, and again in all those places. They soon suppurate and become sores, but prompt treatment will cure glanders in this stage, and save the horse.

During the late war, many good horses contracted nasal gleet from exposure and ill usage, and many of them were destroyed under the impression that they were afflicted with glanders, when they might have been saved had the disease been understood.

Horses known to have glanders should be killed at once, and their stables and harness thoroughly disinfected with chloride of lime. A good washing with carbolic acid will add to the means of safety.

Some years ago, three hundred glandered horses were sent to the veterinary college of Edinburg, Scotland, for experiment. All died but two. These two discharged from both nostrils, while those that died discharged from the left nostril only, and the faculty of the college were of the opinion that the two horses saved did not have glanders. They undoubtedly had nasal gleet, which disease was at the time little understood.—[Kansas City L. S. Indicator.
articles.summary: Reprinted article on the causes, symptoms and prevention of glanders in horses, from the Kansas City Live Stock Indicator.

articles.headline: Angus and Galloway.
articles.text:
Agreeable to my promise of last winter I will try to tell honest inquirers what I believe to be the difference between Galloway and Polled Angus cattle: Let me say in the outset, I have read most of the articles, pro and con, and after searching and studying nearly five years, conclude that if we go far enough back, say to the Feudal age—we shall find that the wild black and polled cattle owned by the wild men of that period and stolen back and forth from each other at every opportunity, were of the self-same, identical breed that Herodotus speaks of, and that have been referred to as Scythian cattle, and that now we classify as follows: The black Polled cattle raised in what is called the Galloway district by the name of Galloways, and the black Polled cattle raised in the northern or Aberdeen and Angus district, and called Aberdeen or Angus cattle.

But I have not told the difference yet between the Galloway and Angus: Well, let me say that a Scotchman on his native heath is like the laws of the Medes and Persians; he seldom, if ever, changes. The ambition of the boys is to do what their fathers did, and in about the same way. Now the Scotchman in southern Scotland, which is the Galloway district, is raising the same kind of cattle (and with a few exceptions, notably, the Duke of Buccleuch, and a few of the best farmers) is trying to raise them as what is called "store" cattle—(we call them stock cattle) by grazing principally, upon as poor land as any man would wish to see. Being near the Gulf stream the climate is not very severe, but cloudy, misty and rainy. This peculiar climate and running out, browsing for a living, is what makes the hair of the Galloway so shaggy, and with poor care and poor feed for generations is probably what makes him so slow a feeder, and in a measure accounts for his absence from the Smithfield fat-stock shows year after year.

I presume every man has concluded there was a great similarity between the breeds. I know I was struck with that fact when I first saw them, and any man who will take the trouble to examine closely, cattle bred by the Duke of Buccleuch will see how very much like the Polled-Angus they are, especially in head and hair. I want to be entirely fair in what I say, and I record myself here as saying I believe that originally the Angus and Galloway were the same wild breed of cattle, and that the distinctive difference in them to-day is, the more and longer skillful mating, feeding and improving by man. The objectionable features have been bred off the Angus to a far greater extent, and the desirable features have been bred on, until to-day they are known as two distinct breeds, and have two distinct books of records for the pedigreed stock. I may say I think that usefulness will be found in both of these breeds, especially in a country like this, where most of our cattle are scrubs, and right here I want to close by saying, that experience will prove to every farmer and cattleman, that horns are a positive detriment in very many ways, and the reader of this article can keep it, to remember, that I say if any man ever handles cattle one season without horns he will forever banish horned cattle from his place.—[G. W. Henry in Kansas City Live-Stock Indicator.
articles.summary: G. W. Henry on the common origin of and differences between Galloway and Polled Angus cattle, reprinted from the Kansas City Live-Stock Indicator.

articles.headline: Commissioners' Meeting.
articles.text:
The first regular meeting of the board of county commissioners toook place on July 1.

Present: Commisioners McKenzie and Goodall and clerk Williamson.

In the absence of Chairman Truscott Goodall was elected chairman pro tem., on motion of McKenzie.

The reading of the minutes of the last meeting was omitted.

The board proceeded to examine and equalize the assessment roll.

On motion, the board adjourned to meet in the morning of July 8, at nine o'clock.

J. C. Williamson, County Clerk.

MEETING ON MORNING OF JULY 8.

Meeting called to order by chairman Goodall.

Present: Commissioners Goodall, McKenzie and Clerk Williamson.

The board proceeded to finish up the equalization of the assessment roll.

On motion, the board adjourned to meet at 7 o'clock this evening and when it adjourns this evening it adjourns to meet again on Tuesday the 13th. of July.

J. C. Williamson, County Clerk.
articles.summary: Billings County commissioners met July 1 and the morning of July 8 to equalize the assessment roll, adjourning to July 13.

articles.text: We regret to say that we have again been misled by rumor into publishing a notice of a marriage that has not taken place. Miss Jennie Morton of South Heart, was the victim of the rumor this time and as we have the same power of divorcing that we have of marrying, we declare the banns to be broken.
articles.summary: The Cow Boy retracts a false marriage notice concerning Miss Jennie Morton of South Heart.

articles.text: The Wells-Fargo Express Co. has stopped business on the Northern Pacific, owing to a decision of a Portland judge that one common carrier is not compelled to carry goods for another common carrier. This decision of course did not affect the whole line, but as goods could not be carried over a part of the road, the express company was compelled to refuse all business.
articles.summary: Wells-Fargo Express stopped business on the Northern Pacific after a Portland court decision.

articles.text: The celebration at Dickinson last Monday was far more of a success than even the most enthusiastic hoped. Except for a strong wind, the day was a perfect one. A procession, consisting of the usual number of riders, both ladies and gentlemen, and a band, a wagon load of goddesses of liberty and a large number of wagons and carriages formed at 9:30. Proceeding to the grand stand at the northern edge of town, several selections were played by the band, "America" was sung and the Declaration of Independence was read by Western Starr. An adjournment for dinner then took place, after which nearly five hundred people assembled at the grand stand to hear speeches from J. A. Rea and Theodore Roosevelt. Mr. Rea was the first speaker and put the audience into a good humor both by his patriotic utterances and quaint anecdotes. Mr. Roosevelt followed with an able discussion on the duties of American citizenship. It was a forcible presentment of high aims a citizen of the United States should keep before him and lacked entirely that spread eagle oratory, with which the speaker said he sympathized deeply. Mr. Roosevelt is essentially a disputant. He gets right at the meat of his subject and in plain, well-chosen words, presents his side of the case in a way that commands attention and wins converts. After the speeches, an adjournment took place to the race track, where the first event was a pony race, Joe McCoul's Blue Jay being barred. Two Indians clothed in little else but modesty took part in the race, one of them "ki-yi-ing" his horse into second place. The next race was a half-mile, free-for-all and was a walk-over for Johnny Goodall's "Splinter." There were about twelve entries of which the most bolted the track, Johnny coming in with a lead of fifty yards, riding side-saddle fashion on a lope and fanning himself with his hat. The next event was the hundred-yard foot race, easily won by a sheep man named Wright, who must spend his spare time running down cayotes. Among the fifteen starters Pat Murn came out a good third. With practice he could make Wright think the tables were turned and the cayotes were after him. In the 200 yard race, Wright again won, Baas of Dickinson second and Murn third.
articles.summary: Report of the Fourth of July celebration at Dickinson on Monday, July 5, with Theodore Roosevelt's oration on the duties of American citizenship, followed by horse and foot races.
